newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico Cetes rates rise on fears of coming month.
newsitem.headline: Mexico Cetes rates rise on fears of coming month.

text.p: With a number of potentially market-moving events coming in the next month, Mexican treasury bills rose sharply at Banco de Mexico's auction on Tuesday.

Markets are concerned about the peso weakening as Mexican borrowers face large amounts of interest payments at the end of the month, the U.S. Federal Reserve meets again to ponder monetary policy, and Mexicans go to the polls on July 6.
The bad case of nerves were enough to push the bellwether one-month rate rose a hefty 113 basis points to 20.43 percent, less than expected, but still a significant hike.
"They (investors) are concerned about volatility in the exchange rate and interest rates, so the markets are covering themselves," ING Barings economist Sergio Martin told Reuters.

The increase was less than expected as a slight recovery in the peso caused upward pressure on rates to ease somewhat during the day. A survey of nine Cetes dealers earlier in the day had forecast the 28-day rate would rise to 20.77 percent.
"Definitely the rise was less than expected, which is good because the trend for rates had been rising quite strongly," Enrique Ramirez, an economist with Santander Investment, told Reuters.
The rate on the one-month paper rose 99 basis points last week after rising 24 basis points the week before that.
Market players are expected to remain wary ahead of the Open Market Committee meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve on July 2, and the July 6 elections in Mexico.
Analysts said, however, that rates could flatten out or even fall even before the elections as market players see a positive outcome to the potentially unnerving events.
ING Barings' Martin forecast that there will be enough dollars in the market to pay interest expenses, and that concerns over the election will calm as the vote approaches.
He said worries over inflationary pressures in the United States could also ease if positive data is released before the next Fed meeting.
"I believe that the market is already attractive enough at these levels in spite of the upcoming elections and I don't think they will rise anymore," Santander's Ramirez said.
In July, Mexicans will vote for a new lower house in Congress, part of the senate, governors in six states and a mayor for Mexico City.

While an opposition candidate is expected to become the new mayor of Mexico City, it is not clear whether the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) will lose control of the lower house of Congress.
